messages.content: Write a post about what a software company learned from a year of remote work. Around 250 words.

**A year without the office**

We closed the office in March. Not as a statement about the future of work — the lease was up and nobody wanted to sign another one mid-pandemic. Twelve months on, here's what actually changed.

Meetings got worse before they got better. For the first quarter we ported the office schedule straight onto Zoom: standup at 9:15, design sync at 11, the Thursday all-hands. By June, calendar time per engineer was up about 40% and we were shipping the same amount. So we killed standup and replaced it with a written thread. Nobody has asked for it back.

Writing turned out to be the whole job. Decisions that used to happen in a hallway and then evaporate now had to survive in a doc, which meant somebody had to make them legible to a person who wasn't there. Every bad incident we had that year traced back to something that was obvious to the team and written down nowhere.

Onboarding broke. We hired eleven people remotely, and the four who struggled most were all early-career — not because they were less capable, but because they had no way to overhear how the work gets done here. New hires now get a named person for their first six weeks. It costs us real engineering time. It costs less than the alternative did.

The thing we got wrong at the start: we treated remote as a logistics problem. It's a documentation problem wearing a logistics costume.

We're not going back. We're also not going to pretend the first six months weren't a mess.

output:
**Twelve months, no office**

We gave up the lease in March. There was no manifesto about the future of work behind it; the term was ending and signing another one that spring felt insane. A year later, here's what actually shifted.

Meetings got worse first. We spent the opening quarter running the office calendar over Zoom: 9:15 standup, design sync at eleven, all-hands on Thursday. By June each engineer was losing roughly 40% more time to calls and shipping the same amount of work. So standup died and became a written thread. Nobody has asked for it back.

Writing turned out to be the job. Choices that used to get made in a corridor and then vanish had to survive in a document instead, which meant someone had to make them make sense to a person who hadn't been standing there. Every bad incident that year traced back to something everyone on the team knew and nobody had typed anywhere.

Onboarding broke outright. Eleven remote hires, and the four who had the hardest time were all early in their careers. Not less capable; they just had no way to overhear how things get done here. New people now get a named person for six weeks. It burns real engineering hours. It burns fewer than the old way did.

What we misread at the start: we thought remote was a logistics problem. It's a documentation problem dressed as one.

We're not going back. We're also not going to pretend the first six months were anything other than a mess.
